The verb charge has many meanings, but they all share one underlying idea: directing something — force, energy, money, or authority — toward a target. Hold onto that idea as you read through each meaning. It will help everything click.
1. To ask for money in return for something

This is the most common everyday meaning. When you charge for something, you demand money as the price of a service or product.

  • "The salon charges ₹500 for a haircut."
  • "The mechanic charged me ₹3,000 for the repair."
  • "How much do you charge per hour?"
  • "They don't charge for delivery."

You can charge a person, or you can charge an amount:

  • "They charged me too much." (charging the person)
  • "They charged ₹200 extra." (charging the amount)
2. To pay using a card or an account (instead of paying cash)

Here, "charge" means to record a purchase against an account — a credit card, a company account, a hotel room, or a running bill.

  • "I'll charge this to my credit card."
  • "He charged the flight to his company account."
  • "Just charge it to my room."

Notice the structure: you charge something to an account. The cost goes into that account to be paid later.
3. To officially accuse someone of a crime

In legal and police contexts, to charge someone means to make a formal, official accusation that they committed a crime. This is not just saying someone did something wrong — it is a legal step taken by authorities.

  • "The police charged him with robbery."
  • "She was charged with fraud."
  • "He was arrested and charged with three counts of assault."

The structure is almost always: charge someone with [crime].

This is a serious, procedural word in this sense. You don't casually "charge" someone; the law does.
4. To rush forward with force; to attack

To charge means to move quickly and powerfully toward something — usually in an attack, a confrontation, or simply an energetic rush. The key feeling is speed + force + direction.

  • Military: "The soldiers charged the enemy position."
  • Animals: "The bull charged at the fence."
  • Sports: "The forward charged toward the goal."
  • Everyday: "The children charged out of school the moment the bell rang."

In basketball, a "charging foul" is when an offensive player runs into a stationary defender — the word is used here in exactly the same way.
5. To fill something with electrical energy

This is the sense you use every day with phones, laptops, and electric vehicles. To charge a device means to supply it with electricity so its battery stores power.

  • "My phone is dead — I need to charge it."
  • "She charged her laptop overnight."
  • "The electric car takes about 8 hours to fully charge."
  • "Is the battery charged yet?" / "Yes, it's fully charged."

The device itself can also "charge" without a direct object — meaning it is receiving power:

  • "Leave it on the table; it's charging."
6. To fill a place, moment, or atmosphere with strong emotion or tension

This is a figurative use — and a very powerful one. When a room, moment, or situation is "charged," it is filled with intense feeling, as if electricity is in the air. You will most often see this in the passive form: "was charged with."

  • "The room was charged with excitement before the match."
  • "The air between them was charged with tension after the argument."
  • "His speech charged the crowd with energy." (He filled the crowd with enthusiasm.)
  • "The atmosphere was charged — something big was about to happen."

This meaning is especially common in literature, journalism, and storytelling. It captures the idea that an emotion is so thick and strong it feels almost physical.
7. To officially give someone a responsibility or task

When you charge someone with something, you formally assign them a responsibility — often with authority, weight, and accountability. The person is now answerable for that task.

  • "The CEO charged her with leading the new division."
  • "The general was charged with defending the border."
  • "I was charged with making sure all guests were registered."
  • "He was charged with the responsibility of managing the funds."

The structure is: charge someone with [task or responsibility].

This is more formal and serious than simply "asking" someone to do something. There is authority and trust behind it.
8. To load or fill something so it is ready for use

This meaning is mostly historical or technical, but you will encounter it in books, science, and industrial contexts. To charge something is to fill it — with fuel, raw material, or ammunition — so it is prepared and ready.

  • Historical: "The soldier charged his musket before the battle." (loaded it with powder and a bullet)
  • Industrial: "Workers charged the furnace with ore."
  • Science: "The chamber was charged with nitrogen gas."

While you may rarely use this meaning yourself, you will recognize it when you come across it.
The Unifying Thread

Here is the single idea behind all eight meanings:

Something is being directed or forced into, at, or onto a target.

MeaningWhat is being directed

When you are billed, a cost is directed at you. When you charge to a card, the cost is directed into an account. When someone is charged with a crime, an accusation is directed at them by the law. When soldiers or animals charge, physical force is directed at a target. When a battery is charged, electrical energy is directed into it. When a room is charged with tension, emotion is directed into the atmosphere. When someone is charged with a duty, responsibility is directed onto them. When a weapon is charged, material is directed into it to make it ready.

One word. Eight flavors. One core idea.
Quick reference: patterns to watch for

• "charge [someone] [amount]" → billing (They charged me ₹500.)
  • "charge [something] to [account]" → using a card/account (Charge it to my card.)
  • "charge [someone] with [crime]" → legal accusation (Charged with theft.)
  • "charge [someone] with [task]" → assigning responsibility (Charged with leading the team.)
  • "charge at/toward [target]" → rushing with force (Charged at the door.)
  • "charge [device]" → powering a battery (Charge your phone.)
  • "charged with [emotion]" → filled with feeling (The room was charged with tension.)
  • "charge [weapon/furnace]" → loading or filling (Charged the furnace.)

Once you internalize these patterns, you will recognize "charge" instantly in any context you ever encounter it.
